title: JP Morgan Chase Q4 earnings: $2.57 a share, vs $2.35 EPS expected
description: Marty Mosby, director of bank strategies at Vining Sparks, and CNBC's Mike Santoli, join "Squawk Box" to give their initial reactions to J.P. Morgan Chase's quarterly earnings results.  J.P. Morgan Chase posted profit and revenue that smashed through analysts' expectations on a strong rebound in trading revenue at the end of 2019.  The bank said Tuesday that fourth-quarter profit rose 21% to $8.52 billion, or $2.57 a share, compared with the $2.35 estimate of analysts surveyed by Refinitiv. Managed revenue climbed 9% to $29.2 billion, compared with the $27.94 billion estimate. Shares of the bank gained 2.1% in midday trading.   CEO Jamie Dimon said the investment bank produced record revenue for a fourth quarter, aided by the rebound in trading revenue from a challenging period a year ago. The strong results in trading helped offset the impact of compressed margins across retail and commercial banking businesses as interest rates dropped.  Profit in the investment bank climbed 48% to $2.9 billion, mainly on trading results. Bond trading revenue surged 86% to $3.4 billion, exceeding the $2.61 billion estimate by roughly $800 million, as fixed-income desks were humming, particularly in securitized products and rates. Stock traders posted a 15% increase in revenue to $1.5 billion, compared with the $1.37 billion estimate.  “JP Morgan Chase produced strong results in the fourth quarter of 2019, capping off a solid year for the firm where we achieved many records, including record revenue and net income,” Dimon said in the release. “While we face a continued high level of complex geopolitical issues, global growth stabilized, albeit at a lower level, and resolution of some trade issues helped support client and market activity towards the end of the year.”  CFO Jennifer Piepszak said last month that trading revenue was “meaningfully” higher in the fourth quarter versus a year earlier. The rebound comes from the industry's' fixed-income trading operations, projected to rise 25% on average, versus a 3% bump in stock trading revenue, KBW analyst Brian Kleinhanzl wrote last month.  In the firm's huge retail banking division, fourth-quarter profit rose 5% to $4.2 billion. While the division's overall revenue climbed 3% to $14 billion, helped by strong credit card and auto loan results, in the core banking business revenue dropped 2% to $6.4 billion as margins shrank on lower interest rates.  The firm's commercial bank posted a 9% drop in profit to $938 million as lower net interest income compressed margins and the bank boosted its provision for credit losses. Asset and wealth management posted a 30% increase in profit to $785 million as rising asset levels boosted results.  Lower interest rates impacted the bank's net yield on interest-earning assets, which fell to 2.38% from 2.55% a year earlier, slightly better than the 2.37% estimate.  J.P. Morgan, the nation's biggest bank by assets, was the first financial institution to report earnings. Later Tuesday, Citigroup reported earnings that exceeded expectations, but Wells Fargo fell short on earnings and revenue.  Bank stocks finished 2019 on a tear, outpacing the broader stock indexes in the fourth quarter as investors rushed into an under-owned sector. J.P. Morgan, in particular, surged last year, climbing about 40%, prompting some analysts to cut their recommendations based on valuation.  But banks face pressure this year as interest rates stay low or are even slashed further. The Federal Reserve cut its benchmark rates for the third time in October, and that pressures banks' net interest income, or the revenue they get from collecting loan payments, minus the interest they pay to depositors.  Here's what Wall Street expected:  Earnings: $2.35 a share, a 19% increase from a year earlier, according to Refinitiv. Revenue: $27.94 billion, a 4.2% increase from a year earlier. asr.full_text: Let me just break in. We're getting some headline flashes on this right now. It looks like the. Fourth quarter number for J.P. Morgan, $2.57 a share. Street had been looking for $2.35. Revenue is better than anticipated. It's $28.3 billion versus the $27.9 billion the street was. Watching for, too. Again, these are just headline flashes, so I can't tell you everything that kind. Of goes into some of these numbers. They do say that the end book value was up 8% to $75.98,. $75.98. Non-interest expense, $16.3 billion. Return on common equity, 14%. Provision for credit losses, $1.43 billion. Mike, what jumps out at you? It sounds all very consistent. Obviously, it's a pretty good margin to beat on the bottom line. You want to see what went into that. The trading line is the one thing we don't know much about. In terms of being able to predict it, but it seems like a good number. The big question,. To Marty's point is just whether the premium being built into JP Morgan after this great run. Is still going to be able to absorb whatever is in these numbers, because it really is pretty high. What's your knee-jerk reaction to that question that Mike just posed? Is there a reason to still. Have a premium in the stock? Well, the reasons is the fact that they're just looked at as the. High-quality, safe place. So when folks rotate back into banks, it's the first place they kind. Of go to. That has to then kind of shake out and send some of the investors down to the more. Discounted stocks like Citigroup at this point is a little bit better valued. Well, and Citigroup has been a huge performer over the last year. I guess that's the result. It's a catch-up, right? It was falling behind in 2018. 2019 has started to catch up,. But still has some farther room to run here in 2020. What's fascinating is JP Morgan, I mean, just in general analyst sentiment, I mean,. You only have about a third of the analysts recommending it right now because the price. And the valuation have gotten up to a point relative to the other banks. So it's just hard. To kind of find a reason for it. This is what's going on in every sector, by the way. The market is just going for the big winners,. The consensus best quality names,. And just building up a premium. But it's almost like Yogi Berra. The place is too crowded, nobody goes there. It kind of seems like that, right. And yet, it looks like it's going to pop on pretty good numbers today. I think you could bank on them talking about the consumers. Very strong. If you believe what the credit market does. As you said that, let me just read the blurb that comes. U.S. consumer continues to be in strong position. That's the flash that hit, as you were saying. Which isn't surprising, but it's still comforting. And I do think that if the corporate credit market, if you look at the way junk bonds and investment-grade bonds are trading,. If that's telling you something important about how long this expansion can go and how long it's going to be until we have to worry about defaults, then banks are okay. I mean, is the corporate debt market telling us that, or is the corporate debt market just kind of aligning itself with Treasury prices? I mean, the spreads to Treasuries are pretty tight. So even relative to Treasuries, it looks like they're – but now the question really, Becky, is,. Is it just that there's this global scarcity of reliable yield and that is causing this kind of high prices and low yields in corporate debt? That's a bigger question. Marty, you want to weigh in there? Yes. We have a credit cycle monitor that actually looks at when we're going to see that cycle turn. Andrew, we've talked in the past and you said, well, you have so many banks on strong buys. Yeah. It was the fact that that discount was coming in and our model was telling us it wasn't going to happen. So we still think that we have a horizon through 2020 and 2021 before we really see that event start to percolate. So we feel confident. That's why the banks, as we got that discount last year, really were one of our, you know, really favorable on our outlook. We've now caught up. And so we now have to kind of look beyond the high quality names and look at some of the ones that are less likely to be the first entry point. What's your top entry level, entry point name? Yeah, like Regions Financial. They have an anomaly on their net interest margin, like we talked about. That's the key thing this quarter. When you roll in the first quarter, they have some interest rate swaps that come on board. That actually will increase their net interest margin when everybody else's is still going down. So it's kind of an anomaly, but their discount with that fundamental fact is one of our favorites. Thank you.
